questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: explain why a throwaway prototype is allowed to be discarded
questions.stem: A food-bank team sketches a shelf-label printer on cardboard in twenty minutes to see whether staff can read labels at arm's length. Why is discarding that sketch an acceptable outcome?

options.text: It settles the label question cheaply, and polished code would cost more to refine than to rewrite
It is not code, so it can never teach anything a conversation could not teach
options.misconception: believes a non-code artifact cannot reveal anything a discussion misses

options.text: Rewriting it later costs nothing, since settled layout decisions stay valid in any language
options.misconception: believes a proven layout transfers into finished code for free

options.text: It proves the printer hardware works, so the label wording needs no further test
options.misconception: believes a cardboard sketch already validates hardware and text

questions.explanation: A throwaway prototype is bought for the answer, not the artifact. The twenty minutes answered the only open question, which is whether staff can read these labels at arm's length, and a real implementation carries costs the sketch never had: driver setup, jam recovery, and label refills. The tempting answer is C, and it is wrong because settled decisions are cheap to re-apply: the team now knows what the labels must say, so rebuilding is typing, not guessing. Treating the cardboard as a foundation is what converts a cheap experiment into an expensive liability.
questions.hint: Ask what the team knows after twenty minutes that it did not know before.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: name the shortcut debt an evolutionary prototype creates
questions.stem: A transit-app team starts with a working route-finder, keeps extending it into the app they ship, and calls the result an evolutionary prototype. What did that choice give up?

options.text: The freedom to throw the code away, because every shortcut now lives in the product
The chance to test the route-finder idea with riders before writing any code
options.misconception: believes an evolutionary prototype somehow skips user testing

options.text: The need to keep the data models consistent as new features are attached
options.misconception: believes prototype code can drift from its models at no cost

options.text: The schedule risk, since an evolutionary prototype always runs longer
options.misconception: believes evolutionary prototypes are inherently slower to build

questions.explanation: An evolutionary prototype is code the team intends to keep, so every shortcut taken to make it finish early stops being a shortcut and becomes a defect waiting for load. Their route-finder hardcodes a route list, has no error state, and assumes one rider at a time; those choices are cheap inside a demo and expensive under real traffic. The tempting answer is C, which names a real nuisance, but a drifting model is only a symptom: the thing actually given up was the option to start clean, and no amount of tidy data models brings that option back.
questions.hint: Ask whether the prototype code was ever intended to be thrown away.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: match prototype fidelity to the question being asked
questions.stem: A school system must decide whether a new cafeteria menu fits on the wall display at a glance. Which prototype should be built first, and why?

options.text: A paper layout taped to the real wall, because only the actual display settles fit and legibility cheaply
A production app, because paper cannot show how the display renders its fonts
options.misconception: believes only production code reveals how a screen will render

options.text: A clickable web mock, because tapping is the only way to test whether text is legible
options.misconception: believes interaction is required in order to test legibility

options.text: No prototype, because a layout question can be settled by reading the source code
options.misconception: believes a visual fit question is answerable from source text

questions.explanation: Fidelity should match the question. Here the question is physical fit and glance-reading, which lives in the real mounting, the real viewing distance, and the real type size, so taped paper on the real wall answers it for a fraction of the cost. The tempting answer is B, and it fails because it answers a different question, font rendering, which the team was not asking; C is the same mistake in a cheaper costume, since tapping tells you nothing about whether a headline reads across a room. Reading the code answers neither, because the property under test is not in the code.
questions.hint: Ask which fidelity reveals the property that is actually in doubt.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: spend a prototype budget on the uncertain part
questions.stem: A team can code the bus-fare calculator in a day, and nobody knows whether riders will read a zone map correctly. Which prototype plan spends the budget best?

options.text: Sketch only the zone map, because the fare arithmetic is already understood and only the map is assumed
Prototype the whole app end to end, since a partial trial can be judged at all
options.misconception: believes a prototype is worthless unless it spans the whole product

options.text: Prototype the fare calculator, since a wrong fare costs the company more than a misread map
options.misconception: believes build cost rather than uncertainty should pick the target

options.text: Prototype nothing and ship both, since riders learn any screen after one journey
options.misconception: believes learnability questions are too cheap to spend a day on

questions.explanation: Prototype cost is scarce, so it belongs on the assumption, not on the certainty. The fare calculator is a known multiplication and comparison that the team can write correctly first try; the zone map is a bet about human reading that only observation can settle. The tempting answer is C, which confuses severity with uncertainty: a wrong fare is worse, but it is not the thing in doubt, so building it first buys nothing and spends the day. Prototyping something already understood is a way of feeling busy while the real risk stays exactly where it was.
questions.hint: Separate the two tasks by what is known and what is assumed.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: trace a throwaway prototype that scans a hardcoded list
questions.stem: A throwaway transit-app prototype holds one hardcoded list and shows the first match it finds. DEFINE seats(list, want): REPEAT each s IN list { IF s.city = want { RETURN s.route } } RETURN "none". seats is called with list = [ {city: "Lima", route: "R7"}, {city: "Oslo", route: "R3"}, {city: "Cusco", route: "R12"} ] and want = "Oslo". Which route does the prototype display?

options.text: R7
options.misconception: reads the table in the wrong order and returns the first row

options.text: R3

options.misconception: assumes the loop always finishes and returns the last row

options.text: none
options.misconception: believes the loop skips the middle row and never matches

questions.explanation: The REPEAT visits rows in stored order: Lima fails the city test, the second row matches Oslo, and the RETURN inside the loop leaves immediately, so the display shows R3. The trap is assuming a REPEAT runs every iteration. Because the RETURN exits on the first match, neither R7 from the opening row nor R12 from the closing row is ever reached, and "none" appears only when the whole list has been scanned without a hit, which is also the real limitation of this hardcoded prototype.
questions.hint: The RETURN sits inside the loop, so decide when the loop stops.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: decide at a prototype time box with incomplete evidence
questions.stem: Two prototype days end and the rough sketch still leaves one open question unsettled. What is the disciplined move at the deadline?

options.text: Stop, decide with the evidence in hand, and record the sketch as a finding to revisit
Extend the deadline by a day, since an unsettled question is not yet an answer
options.misconception: believes a prototype may run past its agreed time box

options.text: Start again from a blank page, since the first sketch is now known to be wrong
options.misconception: believes one inconclusive sketch invalidates the whole approach

options.text: Present the sketch as the settled design, since a prototype needs no sign-off
options.misconception: believes prototypes deserve the same approval as finished work

questions.explanation: A time box exists so the answer arrives while it can still change the plan, and a prototype is judged by the decision it produces rather than by how finished it looks. Two days of evidence plus an open question is a legitimate result: decide on it, write down what the evidence did and did not settle, and let the record point at the next experiment. The tempting answer is B, and it is how prototypes quietly become products, because extending once makes extending twice the norm and the box stops meaning anything.
questions.hint: Ask what the deadline was protecting, not what the sketch still lacks.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: compute how many time-boxed prototypes fit a schedule
questions.stem: A team has 8 days before a demo. It reserves the final 2 days to write up findings, then runs each prototype in a fixed 2-day block with no partial blocks allowed. At most how many prototypes can it run?
questions.explanation: Days left for prototyping are 8 minus the 2 reserved for writing up, so 6 remain, and 6 divided by a full 2-day block gives 3. Checking the other direction, 3 blocks plus 2 write-up days use exactly 8, while 4 blocks plus the same 2 days need 10 and overrun. The tempting answers are 4, which spends the whole 8 days prototyping and forgets the reservation, and 6, which treats a day as a block.
questions.hint: Subtract the reserved days first, then divide by the full block length.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: state what a throwaway prototype leaves behind
questions.stem: A team has finished a throwaway prototype of a cafeteria queue display. In one or two sentences, say what they should keep from it and what they should throw away.

answer.exemplar: Keep the finding: the question asked, the evidence gathered, and the decision that followed. Throw away the sketch, the scaffolding, and any code that existed only to make one assumption visible, because that code carries maintenance cost without carrying a requirement anyone agreed to.

questions.explanation: A prototype's output is knowledge, not software. What survives the bin is the question, the evidence, and the decision, and all three stay useful long after the artifact is gone. The code that made one assumption visible was never a requirement: it hardcodes data, skips error paths, and has no users, so keeping it means importing shortcuts into something that must survive real people. The tempting move is retention because retyping is tiring, but retyping is measured in hours and prototype debt is measured in every future change.
questions.hint: Separate the thing that answered a question from the thing that merely held the answer up.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: design the empty state of a list screen
questions.stem: A school attendance app opens the class list for a class where no student has been enrolled yet. Which screen serves the empty state best?

options.text: One line explaining the class is empty, plus a control to add the first student
A blank table, since an empty result is the most honest rendering of the data
options.misconception: believes an empty result needs no message of any kind

options.text: A loading spinner, since the real roster must still be arriving from the server
options.misconception: believes any blank screen is still a fetch in progress

options.text: A red error banner, since a class with nobody in it is a fault to report
options.misconception: believes validly empty data is an error condition

questions.explanation: An empty state is a designed state, not an accident, and it owes the reader two things: the reason the screen is bare and the action that fills it. A blank table leaves a first-run user unsure whether the app is broken, and a spinner lies by promising data that will never arrive. The tempting answer is D, which treats emptiness as failure, but no enrollment is a normal state for a class created this morning, and flagging it red trains staff to ignore red. A message that explains and a control that acts is the whole job.
questions.hint: Ask what a first-run user would try next if the screen said nothing.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: state what a long-running operation owes the waiting user
questions.stem: A food-bank app starts building a report that takes about 40 seconds to finish. What does the waiting state owe the person who asked for it?

options.text: Visible progress and a way to cancel, because a wait with no exit reads as a freeze
A blank screen, since covering the page with an indicator breaks the layout
options.misconception: believes a progress indicator must never replace page content

options.text: A bare spinner, since naming the step adds nothing while the machine works
options.misconception: believes naming the current step is useless during a long wait

options.text: A success message, since the report will exist as soon as the wait is over
options.misconception: believes promising success early is a harmless shortcut

questions.explanation: The waiting state manages the user's uncertainty, not the machine's progress bar. Forty seconds is long enough that silence reads as a crash, and a spinner with no percentage and no exit gives the reader nothing to predict and no way out when the report is not what they wanted. The tempting answer is D, which feels reassuring and is a lie: a success message shown before the work completes teaches users that confirmations are decorative, so the one message that matters later will not be believed.
questions.hint: Ask what the person knows and what they can do during the wait.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: choose an error state that does not destroy typed work
questions.stem: A long intake form in the food-bank app fails to submit and shows an error. Which choice protects the most of the user's work?

options.text: Keep every field that was typed and mark only the one field that failed its check
Clear the form, so the next attempt starts from known clean values
options.misconception: believes a failed submit should discard what the user typed

options.text: Re-render from the stored draft, dropping the field that failed validation
options.misconception: believes removing the bad field prevents the error from recurring

options.text: Save the values in shared storage and reload a blank form for every visitor
options.misconception: believes a fresh blank form is safer than a failed one

questions.explanation: A failed action should cost the user only the failed action, and on a long form the typed values are the most expensive thing on screen. Keeping everything and flagging one field makes the retry a one-line edit instead of a retyping session, which is the difference between a household being served and walking out. The tempting answer is B, which mistakes tidiness for safety: a cleared form is not clean data, it is lost data, and it will be retyped badly the second time too.
questions.hint: Rank the options by how much retyping each one causes.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: explain why irreversible actions need confirmation
questions.stem: A transit app lets a rider cancel a booked trip. Why must the app ask for confirmation before the booking is removed?

options.text: The trip cannot be restored, so one mistaken tap would destroy the booking outright
Cancelling is slow, so the rider needs a progress bar while it completes
options.misconception: believes a slow action needs a spinner rather than a check

options.text: Confirmation is a legal duty for any change made from a phone screen
options.misconception: believes every mobile change legally requires a confirmation

options.text: Confirming records the cancellation in the app's monthly statistics
options.misconception: believes confirmation exists to log the action for reports

questions.explanation: Confirmation belongs on the actions that are expensive to undo, and a cancelled booking with a seat released to someone else is not undoable at all. One tap in a pocket on a moving bus can destroy a plan that took a week to arrange. The tempting answer is B, which confuses duration with consequence: a fast action can be irreversible and a slow one perfectly safe, and adding a spinner to a confirmation prompt is a common way of appearing careful while destroying the record.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the booking if the rider regrets the tap.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: diagnose why a disabled control drives users away
questions.stem: On a school form the submit button stays greyed out until every required field is filled. A user fills four fields, still sees grey, and leaves. What best explains the exit?

options.text: Nothing on screen names the outstanding requirement, so the rule behind grey is invisible
The button needs a brighter colour before the page will let the user press it
options.misconception: believes the refusal to accept a press is a contrast problem

options.text: The four entries were stored as text, so the form cannot count them as filled
options.misconception: believes the type a value is stored as blocks a filled count

options.text: The user never scrolled down, so the remaining fields were hidden off screen
options.misconception: believes the cause is where the fields sit on the page

questions.explanation: A control that refuses input owes an explanation, and a disabled button with no stated requirement is indistinguishable from a broken one. The user filled what they could see, saw no change, and had no way to learn which field was still wanted. The tempting answer is D, which is a real possibility on a long form, but it predicts a user who scrolls and then leaves, not a user who filled four fields and stopped. A disabled control that names its condition, or a live count of what remains, converts an unexplained refusal into a task.
questions.hint: Weigh the hypotheses: which one leaves the user with no way forward?

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: show the age of displayed data when it may be stale
questions.stem: A transit app shows arrival times last fetched eleven minutes ago, and the next bus is due any second. What does the screen owe the rider?

options.text: A mark that the times may be out of date, with a way to refresh them now
The same times, unlabelled, because replacing numbers every few seconds confuses
options.misconception: believes changing numbers harms readers more than old numbers do

options.text: An empty arrival panel, since an unknown time is worse than a listed one
options.misconception: believes hiding data is always the safer display choice

options.text: The same times in bold, since confident presentation makes them more reliable
options.misconception: believes visual confidence makes aged values trustworthy

questions.explanation: Displayed data has an age, and eleven minutes is long enough on a city route that a bus can have arrived, turned, and gone. Marking the staleness lets the rider decide how much to trust the screen, and offering a refresh makes the recovery theirs. The tempting answer is D, which mistakes emphasis for accuracy: bold text raises confidence in a number without adding a single minute of information, and a rider who has been stranded once will distrust every arrival time the app shows.
questions.hint: Ask what the rider would do differently if the times were known to be old.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: trace guarded transitions through a screen state machine
questions.stem: A list screen has one state variable. DEFINE step(state, event): IF event = "load" { IF state = "empty" { RETURN "loading" } } IF event = "fail" { IF state = "loading" { RETURN "error" } } IF event = "open" { IF state = "list" { RETURN "list" } IF state = "error" { RETURN "list" } } RETURN state. The screen starts in state "empty" and the events arrive in the order load, fail, open, load. Which state is on screen after the last event?

options.text: list
loading
options.misconception: believes a load event restarts the fetch from any state

options.text: error
options.misconception: believes the retry is only accepted from the list state

options.text: empty
options.misconception: believes every event resets the screen to its default

questions.explanation: Every branch is guarded, so state is carried forward: load is only accepted from empty, so the screen becomes loading; fail is only accepted from loading, so it becomes error; the retry open is accepted from error, so it becomes list; the final load arrives while the screen is already list, and since load requires empty it falls through to the last RETURN and the list stays. The tempting answer is loading, which treats load as an unconditional restart and is exactly how a screen ends up spinning over data it already has.
questions.hint: Work through the four events in order and check each guard's precondition.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: name the three parts an error message must carry
questions.stem: A user taps Save on the school app and the screen does not change. Which three parts must the message carry to be any use?

options.text: What failed, why it failed, and what the user can do next about it
The error code, the release version, and the support desk opening hours
options.misconception: believes diagnostic detail helps the person who pressed save

options.text: The stack trace, the failing line number, and the name of the developer
options.misconception: believes developer internals serve the end user in a message

options.text: An apology, the expected wait time, and a link to the request status
options.misconception: believes courtesy plus a status link replaces telling the user what to do

questions.explanation: An error message is a handoff from the program to a person who has to fix something, so it must name the failure, explain the cause, and hand back an action. A user who knows the file was too big and the limit is 8 MB can solve it alone; a user who knows only that an error occurred must open a second tool and describe what they already did. The tempting answer is D, which is warm and useless, because feeling sorry and waiting are not steps towards a saved file.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader must know to fix it without contacting anyone.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: write an error message that describes a fix rather than blaming
questions.stem: A signup rejects a card number. Which message is written for the person who pressed the button?

options.text: That card number has 15 digits and card numbers carry 16, so check it and resubmit
You typed the card number wrong; please be more careful and try again
options.misconception: believes scolding the reader prevents the mistake next time

options.text: The card field failed validation under rule CV-14, so consult the handbook
options.misconception: believes quoting a validation rule is a user-facing explanation

options.text: Payment could not be processed at this time; please try again later today
options.misconception: believes a generic retry line is enough without naming the cause

questions.explanation: Describe the condition and the repair, never the person. This message reports what the value is, what it should be, and what to do next, so the user can find the missing digit in seconds. The tempting answer is B, and it fails twice: shaming makes people quit rather than correct, and it still does not say which digit is wrong. C hides behind a rule number that means nothing outside the codebase, and D is honest but gives the reader nothing to act on before the day ends.
questions.hint: Look for the option that states the condition and the next step, with no judgement.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: explain why a bare error code is not a message
questions.stem: A school portal shows the single line "ERR_5031" where a form failed to save. What is the design fault?

options.text: The code names the failure to a maintainer but tells the user nothing to act on
The code is too long, so a shorter string would explain the failure better
options.misconception: believes brevity rather than meaning makes a message fail

options.text: The code is not in plain words, so real language would resolve the failure
options.misconception: believes a code lacks information only because it is not prose

options.text: The code sits alone, since embedding it in a sentence would supply the missing meaning
options.misconception: believes grammar around a code supplies its explanation

questions.explanation: An identifier is a lookup key for whoever maintains the system, not a sentence for the person it blocked. ERR_5031 tells a teacher nothing about whether the filename was wrong, the disk was full, or the network dropped, so the only move left is a support ticket. The tempting answer is C, which is half right for the wrong reason: prose helps, but only when the prose carries the condition and the next step. The code belongs in a detail line under a human message, not in place of one.
questions.hint: Ask who can act on the information this line contains.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: select the error message that lets the user self-check
questions.stem: A batch upload of 12 files fails. Which message lets the user act without asking for help?

options.text: Three files were too large; the biggest was 9 MB against the 8 MB limit
The upload failed; please check your files and your connection, then retry
options.misconception: believes a retry suggestion is enough without naming the cause

options.text: Upload error 7 occurred while the batch moved to the storage service
options.misconception: believes a service level name explains the problem to the user

options.text: Some files could not be uploaded at this time; the team has been notified
options.misconception: believes an apology plus a ticket is a complete explanation

questions.explanation: A message that names the affected items, a measured value, and the threshold lets the user check one condition and fix it. This one says which files, how big the worst one is, and what the limit is, so the next upload succeeds without a support ticket. The tempting answer is B, which sounds thorough and gives the user two things to check instead of one, which is a longer hunt that often ends the same way. C describes where the failure happened, not what to do, and D hands the problem to staff.
questions.hint: Look for the option containing a measured value and the limit it exceeded.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: explain why protocol vocabulary fails an end user
questions.stem: A transit app shows "HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity" to a rider whose address is missing a postcode. Why does the message fail?

options.text: It names an internal protocol state instead of the postcode the rider must add
It is too short, so the app should print the whole server response instead
options.misconception: believes a longer technical message is more useful to a rider

options.text: It appears before the form is filled in, so it arrives earlier than it should
options.misconception: believes when a message shows matters more than what it says

options.text: It names the address field, so the rider already knows what to correct
options.misconception: reads a protocol term as if it were a plain field name

questions.explanation: Speak the reader's language, and start from their goal. The rider needs a postcode, and 422 is a category label that only an engineer can act on, so the message transfers work to the user without moving it forward. The tempting answer is B, which assumes more text means more help; a full response body is still protocol vocabulary, just longer, and it makes the rider feel stupid for asking. The rule is simple: if the message only makes sense to whoever wrote the code, it is a log line, not a message.
questions.hint: Ask what the rider must change, and whether the wording names it.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: rewrite a failing message to the three-part test
questions.stem: The food-bank intake app shows only "Validation failed." when a volunteer submits a household with no address. Rewrite that message so it passes the three-part test, in one or two sentences.

answer.exemplar: "No address was entered, so this household cannot be saved. Add a street address and submit again." It names what failed, which is the missing address; why it matters, which is that nothing is stored without it; and the next action, which is to add the address and resubmit.

questions.explanation: The original fails all three parts. It does not say which field is missing, it does not say that the save is blocked, and it does not say what would clear it, so the volunteer is left holding a household record that does not exist. The tempting repair is to keep the sentence and add an exclamation mark or an apology, but tone is not information: a warmer message with no content still leaves the volunteer guessing. A message earns its place only when the reader can act on it without opening anything else.
questions.hint: Check the draft for the field, the consequence, and the action.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: choose a thin vertical slice for the first increment
questions.stem: A school system must let parents see their child's grade. Which first increment delivers the most learning per day spent?

options.text: One class, one parent login, one real grade, wired from storage through to the screen
The full storage design for every class, since nothing can be saved without it
options.misconception: believes a first slice must cover all the storage it will ever need

options.text: Every parent's notification preference, since grades cannot be trusted without it
options.misconception: believes notification settings must arrive before any visible grade

options.text: Logins for all schools at once, since a grade is useless without complete access
options.misconception: believes full coverage of login must be the first slice shipped

questions.explanation: A slice is thin and vertical: it crosses every layer once, so the risky integration is exercised while the breadth stays small. One class and one parent proves that a grade can be stored, secured, and shown, which is the question the project actually faces. The tempting answer is B, and it is the standard way slices die: building one layer completely teaches you that the layer works, never that the layers fit together, and by the time the second layer is done the first has already changed.
questions.hint: Ask which option exercises the risky seam between layers earliest.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: detect an increment that ships no working behaviour
questions.stem: An increment is described as "a new search box, but disabled until the ranking code lands next week." What breaks the promise of incremental delivery?

options.text: The release has no working behaviour of its own, so nobody gains anything usable
The box is visually unfinished, so users will see it as an unpolished product
options.misconception: believes visual polish is what makes an increment shippable

options.text: The ranking code is scheduled late, so the team is not really working in small pieces
options.misconception: believes small pieces are defined by who writes them, not by what ships

options.text: The box is behind a feature flag, so no one can try the new search yet
options.misconception: believes a control nobody can press still counts as delivered value

questions.explanation: Every increment must leave the product working and better, so a release whose new control does nothing is a promise with no behaviour behind it. The team either ships a search that works on today's simple ranking, which is useful now and can be improved, or it holds the control until it can. The tempting answer is D, which thinks a feature flag is a delivery mechanism; hiding work removes the feedback that incremental delivery exists to collect, so a flag that hides the only new thing ships nothing and learns nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what a user can do after this release that they could not do before.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: trace one pass of a dependency-aware slice builder
questions.stem: A build script groups features into releasable slices in one forward pass. DEFINE slices(features, done): out <- []; REPEAT each f IN features { ready <- TRUE; REPEAT each need IN f.needs { IF need NOT IN done AND need NOT IN out { ready <- FALSE } } IF ready { APPEND f.id TO out } } RETURN out. Features in list order are B needs A, A needs nothing, C needs nothing, D needs B. done starts empty. How many features does the routine return, and which are they?

options.text: 2 features, A and C
4 features, every one of them
options.misconception: believes every feature clears the readiness check on its first pass

options.text: 3 features, A, C, and D
options.misconception: believes any feature whose need is named at all is treated as ready

options.text: 1 feature, A alone
options.misconception: believes a second feature with no needs is somehow blocked

questions.explanation: The check asks whether a need is already in done or already in the list being built, so a feature that appears before its need is skipped and never revisited. B comes first and needs A, which has not been added yet, so B is dropped; A and C need nothing and are appended; D needs B, which was never added, so D is dropped too. The tempting answer is all four, which treats one forward pass as if it were a fixed-point solver, and that is a real design smell here: the list must be ordered so needs come first, or the routine must run again.
questions.hint: Process the list in order and check each need against done and out.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: order increments around dependencies rather than importance
questions.stem: A food-bank app must ship reminders, which need a phone number, plus phone capture and reports. Which order respects the dependency and still ships something useful first?

options.text: Phone capture, then reminders, then reports, because each piece needs the one before it
Reminders, then phone capture, then reports, because reminders matter most to staff
options.misconception: believes importance outranks a technical dependency in the order

options.text: Reports, then reminders, then phone capture, because reporting comes first in policy
options.misconception: believes a policy document sets the order of the technical work

options.text: Phone capture, then reports, then reminders, because donors read the reports
options.misconception: believes audience size decides the order with no dependency check

questions.explanation: Order work so each increment's inputs already exist. Reminders cannot function without a stored number, so capture ships first, and a report is genuinely useful as soon as there are households to report on. The tempting answer is B, which lets a stated preference override a hard dependency and produces a reminder feature that has nothing to read from on day one. Importance is the right tie-breaker between two available orders, never a way to sequence something that cannot yet work.
questions.hint: Find the item with no requirement of its own and start there.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: count the slices unblocked after a delivery
questions.stem: A transit app splits into 6 slices. Slices A, C, and D need nothing built first, B needs A, E needs B, and F needs C. After A and C have shipped, how many further slices are unblocked and ready to deliver?
questions.explanation: The delivered set is now A and C. Checking each remaining slice against it: B needs A, which has shipped, so B is unblocked; D needs nothing, so it is unblocked; E needs B, which has not shipped, so E stays blocked; F needs C, which has shipped, so F is unblocked. That gives 3, cross-checked as 6 slices minus the 2 already delivered minus the 1 still blocked. The tempting answer of 4 counts E, because its need is named in the plan even though that need does not exist yet.
questions.hint: For each undelivered slice, ask whether every need is already delivered.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: weigh the cost of speculative generality against one real case
questions.stem: A team has one delivery partner, a known courier, and is asked to make routing pluggable for any future courier. What is the real cost of that request?

options.text: A general interface must be designed and tested against a case that does not exist yet
A single courier shows no pattern, so a general design has nothing to model
options.misconception: believes a design is impossible without several existing examples

options.text: Pluggable designs run slower than direct calls in every measured comparison
options.misconception: believes generality is a runtime performance problem not a build cost

options.text: Future couriers will demand changes, so the interface breaks the day it ships
options.misconception: believes the interface must break as soon as a second party appears

questions.explanation: Build for the case in hand. A pluggable routing layer has to be designed, documented, and tested, and its only test is a hypothetical second courier who may never sign, so the team pays for certainty it cannot receive. The tempting answer is B, which is a fair worry about thin evidence but leads to paralysis: one real case is enough to design for, and the cost of being wrong later is a later refactor. Every extra branch is also a new place the single real courier can now fail.
questions.hint: Ask what the flexibility buys today, and what it costs to carry.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: compare total cost of ownership rather than build days
questions.stem: Two features are proposed for the food-bank app. Feature A takes 1 build day and needs a monthly fixing session forever. Feature B takes 4 build days and is never touched again. Over a year, which is the cheaper thing to own?

options.text: Feature B, because 4 build days beat 1 build day plus twelve monthly sessions
Feature A, because the smaller build is cheaper on the day it ships
options.misconception: believes only first day build effort belongs in a comparison

options.text: They cost the same, because ownership only counts once a feature has launched
options.misconception: believes running cost is irrelevant after the launch date

options.text: Feature A, because twelve short monthly sessions cost under one build day
options.misconception: believes upkeep is free because each individual session is quick

questions.explanation: Compare total cost of ownership, not the number on the estimate sheet. Twelve monthly sessions plus the first build day outlast four days of building, so A is the more expensive asset even though it looked like the bargain. The tempting answer is D, and it is right about each session being short and wrong about the sum: short and repeated is still recurring, and each session also pulls someone away from planned work. If the monthly fix is truly minutes and truly rare, count those minutes honestly before deciding.
questions.hint: Add the recurring sessions to the build day before comparing the two.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: explain why repeated small concessions consume a schedule
questions.stem: Over six weeks a stakeholder adds six "one-hour" changes and the team says yes to each. What is the real cost of the pattern?

options.text: The small requests eat the schedule and the originally promised feature never ships
The team grows rude, since every extra request deserves a polite refusal instead
options.misconception: believes saying yes to every small ask is the cost being counted

options.text: The requests get logged, so recording them proves the team is being responsive
options.misconception: believes writing a request down cancels the time it consumes

options.text: Only the first is a real change, since the later five repeat the same request
options.misconception: believes a repeated request costs nothing after the first one

questions.explanation: Small concessions are not small in aggregate, and a request list with no priority order and no cost attached is exactly how a schedule disappears. Six one-hour asks are six hours, plus the switching cost of leaving whatever each one interrupted, which is usually larger than the hour itself. The tempting answer is C, which confuses recording a cost with paying it: the log gets longer while the promised feature does not. Saying yes is a decision with a price, and a decision with a price needs an owner.
questions.hint: Add the hours up, then ask what each interruption cost the work in progress.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: separate a hard constraint from a negotiable preference
questions.stem: A transit app must never lose a rider's saved payment details, and a designer wants a purple theme. Which statement about the cut list is correct?

options.text: The payment rule is a constraint and stays; the theme is a preference that can wait
Both are requirements, since the designer asked for one as firmly as the other
options.misconception: believes the confidence of the asker sets a requirement's status

options.text: The theme stays, since a lost card is less urgent than a dull screen
options.misconception: believes visual appeal can outrank data integrity in a cut

options.text: Both may go, since requirements are negotiable once a deadline is at risk
options.misconception: believes every requirement is negotiable under deadline pressure

questions.explanation: Separate constraints from preferences before any negotiation, because a constraint is a line that cannot move and a preference is a candidate being weighed. Data that must not be lost is a constraint no schedule can bend; the theme is a preference, and dropping it costs nothing but taste. The tempting answer is B, which turns loudness into status: a constraint does not become negotiable because a designer stated it confidently, and a cut list built on volume rather than kind is how teams cut the wrong line first.
questions.hint: Ask which requirement can be violated without making the product wrong.
